etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Adjectivization of 稚児(ややこ) (yayako, “infant”), from the way infants are fretful and complicated to deal with.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with the adjective 激しい (hageshii). Possibly from はげ (hage, root of 激しい) + む (-mu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 幽靈 /幽灵 (ʔjiw leng, literally “dark + supernatural”). Compare modern Mandarin reading yōulíng, Min Nan iu-lêng.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 志す (kokorozasu, “to intend to do something, to aspire to do something”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 心 (kokoro, “heart; mind”) + 指す (sasu, “to point”), literally in reference to where one's thoughts are focused on.
First cited to the mid-900s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 欲 is a daiyōji replacing 慾.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Dictionaries generally consider this equivalent to or a shift from a compound of 日(か) (ka, “day”) + 読(よ)み (yomi, “reading; counting”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 読(よ)む (yomu, “to read; to count”)). Literally, “day counting”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, first appearing in the Kojiki of 712 CE; ultimately from Proto-Japonic *imanta. Cognate with Okinawan なーだ (nāda, “yet”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tadajopu/ → /tadajoɸu/ → /tadajou/
From Old Japanese. First cited to the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 生(う)まれ (umare) + 付(つ)き (tsuki).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tikusjau/ → /t͡ɕikusjoː/
From Middle Chinese 畜生 (MC trhjuwH sraeng, literally “livestock + livestock; sacrificial animal”), itself influenced by Sanskrit तिर्यञ्च् (tiryañc, “a beast; the organic world”) or Sanskrit तिर्यग्योनि (tiryagyoni, “animal creation”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 略 is a daiyōji replacing 掠.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 議決 (ngjeᴴ kwet).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/koːnipu/ → /koːniɸu/ → /koːniu/ → /koːnjuː/
From Middle Chinese compound 購入 /购入 (kuwᴴ nyip, literally “present, give + enter”). Compare modern Cantonese reading kau³ jap⁶.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, stem or continuative form) of the classical verb 傾る (nadaru), modern 雪崩れる, 傾れる (nadareru, “to slope, descend; of snow, to slide”).
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), borrowed from Chinese 雪崩 (xuěbēng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/uwo/ → /uo/
From Old Japanese.
Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *uwo.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/uwo/ → /iwo/ → /io/
Alteration of older uo, appearing from roughly the Heian period. Alternatively this might be the usage of an apophonic form *iwo; compare Proto-Ryukyuan *iwo.
Still used today in some dialects.
